verdicts.summary: The note's real hazard is that a visitor who is not the owner, or who cannot reach the relay, ends on an error with no code fallback. Finding 0 already states this. The cross-origin call itself holds up: it sends no cookies, CORS allows the DPoP headers, and the relay session carries the full standard scopes.
verdicts.scenario: An owner who once paired a browser on the tunnel host still has a cookie there, and the cookie would beat DPoP in selectRequestCredential. It is not sent: DPoP requests skip credentials:'include' (environmentHttpAuth.ts:50-54), so the server sees only the DPoP header.

verdicts.summary: The redirect logic matches the code, and the test covers the tunnel, other-host and peer-link cases. The dead end for visitors who are not the owner is finding 0. A crafted hosted link that names a peer-link client is not new: approve() never checked peerLink on a session decision, before or after this change.
The bound holds. The decision POST is never resent by the renew-and-retry loop, because a decision with bad credentials comes back as a refusal, not an invalid_credential error.
verdicts.scenario: Tried: a stale DPoP token on the decision call triggers the retry and mints two auth codes. It does not. approvingSession swallows every auth error (orElseSucceed undefined), approve() turns that into McpOAuthPageError and then AuthMcpApprovalError, and the client catches it as 'refused'. So the invalid_credential retry at environmentHttpAuth.ts:233-240 never fires for a decision. The approval-read retry is bounded to one try, inside the 10s timeoutOrElse.

verdicts.summary: The client filter accepts everything the server can emit. The server only emits https redirects or http on a loopback host, and the client's loopback set is a superset of the server's.
verdicts.scenario: Tried: a redirect to http://[::1]:port/cb, and to http://localhost/cb. Server side, url.hostname is '[::1]' or 'localhost', which are in LOOPBACK_HOSTNAMES. Client side, isLoopbackHost accepts '[::1]' and 'localhost' (and also 0.0.0.0). So no legitimate redirect is refused, and javascript:/data: URLs cannot be registered.

verdicts.summary: Approve, by click or by Enter, stays gated on `armed`. Re-arming is triggered only by focus and visibility changes on the window itself, not by focus moving inside the page.
verdicts.scenario: Tried: pressing Enter in the form right after details load, and right after switching back to the tab. onSubmit calls decide only when canApprove is true, and canApprove requires armed, which the 700ms timer sets. The listener sits on window without capture, so focus events on elements (they do not bubble) do not reset it while the user clicks the radios.

verdicts.summary: Open question answered: a policy that keeps remote clients out also turns T3 Connect off. CloudLink then unlinks, linkState is not linked, and /authorize never sends anyone to the hosted page, so the policy is not bypassed. The separate fallback-without-a-code hazard is finding 7.
verdicts.scenario: Tried: a managed policy with limits.clients lacking 'remote', and an agent that reaches the tunnel's /oauth/mcp/authorize and is sent to the hosted page for a one-click approve. allowsConnect is false, so at startup CloudLink unlinks and only offers linkState and unlink (CloudLink.ts:1627-1646). Connect-paired sessions are revoked (EnvironmentAuth.ts:1446). hostedApprovalUrl needs state.linked, so it returns none, and there is no tunnel to reach.

verdicts.summary: The note says every non-success becomes ConnectMcpApprovalUnavailableError and then a user-facing message. Finding 1 already reports that this collapses timeout and not-owner into one wording and leaves the other branch dead. The transport and auth parts check out: no cookies are sent, CORS allows the DPoP headers, and the Connect token has AuthStandardClientScopes, so csrfToken and oneClickAccess come back.
